add e2b provider

e2b: friendlier server type, quieter run, no cfg mutation

- prefer sandbox.Alias over sandbox.TemplateID so list/status display
  the human label ("base") instead of the internal template GUID.
- suppress the redundant "exit status N" mirror that envd echoes via
  the End.Error field on every non-zero exit; only print Error when
  the process did not exit normally (signals, oom, exec failures).
- compute the template once into a local; stop mutating cfg.ServerType
  inside createSandbox so the backend's stored config is untouched.

Live smoke (E2B production):
  warmup -> cbx_b33d45bb636d / sandbox=i0v482ipj3g8yez2c17qs (472ms)
  list   -> server_type.name="base" (was "rki5dems9wqfm4r03t7g")
  status -> type=base ready=true
  run    -> uname -a exit=0; bash -c 'exit 7' propagates host_exit=7
  stop   -> released; list -> []; raw API GET /sandboxes -> []

fix(hetzner): unmarshal private_net as array (best-effort) instead of crashing

Hetzner returns `private_net` as an array of network attachments (per the
documented schema at docs.hetzner.cloud/#servers-get-all-servers), but the
Server struct modeled it as a single struct. Every Hetzner-backed command
hit `json: cannot unmarshal array into Go struct field
Server.servers.private_net ...` on the first server in the list response,
breaking `list`, `doctor`, `warmup`, and `run --id ...` for any account
with at least one server.

Promoted `PrivateNet` to a named type with a best-effort `UnmarshalJSON`
that accepts both shapes:

  - Array (Hetzner): lifts the first attachment's `ip` into
    `PrivateNet.IPv4.IP`, so any caller that wants a private-network IP
    for a Hetzner-leased box still gets one. Empty array stays empty.
  - Struct (legacy `{"ipv4": {"ip": "..."}}`): kept for backward
    compatibility with anything that round-trips Server via JSON outside
    the Hetzner API (test fixtures, snapshots).

Azure / Proxmox are unaffected — they populate the field via direct
field assignment (azure.go:903, proxmox.go:605), never JSON. Access
patterns like `server.PrivateNet.IPv4.IP = ip` continue to work because
the underlying struct shape is unchanged.

Regression tests cover four shapes: empty array, attached array (asserts
first-attachment IP), legacy struct, and null/omitted.

Repro before the fix:

    $ HCLOUD_TOKEN=... crabbox list
    json: cannot unmarshal array into Go struct field
    Server.servers.private_net of type struct { IPv4 struct ... }

feat: add runpod provider

Adds the RunPod (https://runpod.io) SSH-lease provider. The provider
deploys a CPU pod through the RunPod GraphQL API, waits for
runtime.ports[] to expose the public TCP mapping for port 22, then hands
Crabbox a normal SSH target so sync/run/ssh/stop reuse the existing
transports.

Auth is via RUNPOD_API_KEY (CRABBOX_RUNPOD_API_KEY overrides), never a
flag. Doctor verifies auth with a myself query and inventory with
myself.pods without ever calling a mutation.

The lease is ephemeral: pod is created on Acquire (defaulting to the
cheapest documented cpu3c-2-4 flavor on runpod/base:0.6.2) and
terminated on ReleaseLease via podTerminate.

fix(cli): accept --id on stop and auto-route static_ leases

Before, two cliffs after warmup:

1. crabbox stop required the lease id as a trailing positional and rejected
   --id, the same flag every other lease command uses. Run's emitted
   stop_command was the only crabbox-emitted command users could not paste
   back verbatim.
2. crabbox run/status/stop and friends silently fell back to the default
   coordinator provider when only --id <slug> was passed, so a static SSH
   lease (provider=ssh, lease id static_<host>) failed with provider auth
   errors until the user re-typed --provider ssh --static-host ... .

This change:

- Adds --id to crabbox stop (positional still accepted) and updates the
  printed stop_command to emit --id <lease>.
- Adds autoRouteStaticLease, applied by both loadLeaseTargetConfig and
  applyLeaseCreateFlagsForLease, so a lease id with the static_ prefix
  routes to provider=ssh and derives --static-host from the suffix when
  the user has not set either flag explicitly. Explicit --provider or
  --static-host wins.

Reproduces the original symptom and confirms the fix on a static SSH
lease against a remote macOS host.

feat(sync): add sync.include whitelist (#210)

* feat(sync): add sync.include whitelist

Sync currently only supports excludes (a blacklist). For a large repo where you
only want a few paths in the box — e.g. running a proof/test job that needs just
`src/` and `scripts/` out of a working tree full of unrelated data — blacklisting
every junk directory is fragile and never-ending.

Add `sync.include`: when set, only paths matching an include pattern are synced
(after excludes). Filtering happens inside the manifest walker so the size
preflight sees the trimmed set (a 136 GiB working tree becomes the few hundred MB
you actually selected). Matching mirrors excludes — an include of `src` keeps
`src` and everything under it, a file path keeps that exact file, and globs match.

- `SyncConfig.Includes` + YAML `sync.include` / `sync.includes`
- include-aware `syncManifestFiltered` (syncManifest stays a thin wrapper, so
  existing callers/tests are unchanged); deleted/changed walkers honor includes too
- `pathIncluded` helper; wired through fingerprint/run/actions/sync-plan paths
- tests for the manifest whitelist and the matcher; docs

* fix(sync): expose sync.include in config show

ClawSweeper: the whitelist could be active while `config show` and `config show
--json` omitted it, making effective sync config misleading during troubleshooting.
Add `include` to the structured sync view and an `includes=<n>` count to the text
output, with a config-show regression covering both.

Add a new local-vm family provider that creates and manages Windows
virtual machines via Microsoft Hyper-V on Windows hosts. The provider
uses PowerShell commands (New-VM, Set-VM, Start-VM, Stop-VM, Remove-VM)
for the full VM lifecycle and connects to guests over SSH via the
built-in Windows OpenSSH server.

applyFlags now checks flagWasSet(target) to distinguish explicit
CLI flags from baseConfig defaults. Explicit --target linux or
--target macos fails closed for provider=hyperv. The baseConfig
linux default (no --target flag) still converts to windows silently.

applyDefaults reverted to only handle empty TargetOS; the linux->windows
conversion moved to applyFlags where flag-explicitness is available.

* fix: keep Hyper-V lease disk/VM files off the system drive

Two issues surfaced during a live smoke on a space-constrained host:

- Resize-VHD blindly shrank the copied template to the requested
  --hyperv-disk size, corrupting disks whose template virtual size was
  larger (the MS dev VHDX is 125 GB vs the 50 GB default). Guard with
  Get-VHD so the template is only ever grown, never shrunk, and fail
  fast (cleaning up the copy) if Hyper-V can't read it.

- New-VM defaulted VM configuration/runtime files (incl. the multi-GB
  .VMRS memory file) to C:\ProgramData even when the VHD lived on
  another drive, so Start-VM failed on a full C:. Pass New-VM -Path a
  dedicated VM dir under the same Hyper-V home as the VHD so both follow
  USERPROFILE redirection.

Adds unit tests for the resize guard and the New-VM -Path placement.

* fix: apply tart-provider lessons to harden Hyper-V provider

Port the robustness fixes from the merged tart provider (PR #209) that
apply to Hyper-V:

- applyDefaults now inherits an explicit --ssh-user when --hyperv-user is
  unset, instead of unconditionally forcing the "crabbox" guest user
  (mirrors tart's applyDefaults).
- doctor now reports the configured image (image=...) for parity with the
  tart doctor output, so it's clear which VHDX template the provider will
  use.
- removeVM surfaces a VHDX-deletion failure as a warning rather than
  silently swallowing it, so an orphaned lease disk is visible. It stays
  non-fatal so ReleaseLease still prunes the lease claim (the VM is
  already gone by then).

Other tart lessons (keep=true post-start preservation, createVM failure
cleanup incl. the copied VHDX, crabbox-only inventory filtering, empty-IP
erroring) were already present in the provider and verified during this
pass.

Adds tests for the ssh-user inheritance and the doctor image field.

* fix: prevent Hyper-V lease disk leak from automatic checkpoints

Surfaced by a live warm on Windows 11 client Hyper-V: the lease VM
started fine and ran from D:, but `crabbox stop` left the 42 GB base
VHDX behind.

Cause: client Hyper-V enables automatic checkpoints by default, so
Start-VM creates a <name>_<guid>.avhdx differencing disk and attaches it
in place of the base VHDX. removeVM only deleted the attached disk when
its path equalled the base <name>.vhdx, so the base disk (and the per-VM
config directory) leaked on every release.

- Disable automatic checkpoints on lease VMs (Set-VM
  -AutomaticCheckpointsEnabled $false); they are ephemeral and have no
  use for checkpoints.
- removeVM now always deletes the base VHDX, sweeps any name-prefixed
  differencing disks in the VHD dir (leaving unrelated attached disks
  untouched), and removes the per-VM config directory New-VM -Path
  creates.

Adds regression tests for both.

* fix: reject explicit non-Windows target from config/env, not just CLI

applyFlags only rejected a conflicting target when it came from the
`--target` CLI flag; a non-Windows target set via YAML (`target:`/
`targetOS:`) or env (`CRABBOX_TARGET`/`CRABBOX_TARGET_OS`) fell through to
the silent linux->windows rewrite instead. Gate on
core.IsTargetExplicit(cfg) as well so an explicitly-set non-Windows
target from any source is rejected, while a never-set target still
adopts the provider's native windows.

Adds tests for the YAML/env explicit-target cases.

* feat: install OpenSSH in the guest so templates need only an admin password

The provider previously required a VHDX template with OpenSSH already
installed and configured, but shipped no way to produce one -- the main
adoption barrier for the Hyper-V provider (cloud providers bootstrap the
guest via cloud-init; tart images ship SSH-ready).

Bridge that gap: during Acquire, over the PowerShell Direct channel the
provider already uses for key injection, install and start the Windows
OpenSSH server when it isn't present and open the firewall. This drops
the template requirement to a plain Windows VHDX with a known
administrator password (CRABBOX_HYPERV_GUEST_PASSWORD) -- the irreducible
minimum, since PowerShell Direct needs a credential to connect.

Refactors the PowerShell-Direct credential/retry boilerplate into a
shared invokeInGuest helper used by both ensureOpenSSH and injectSSHKey.
Adds tests; updates the requirement messages.

* docs: hyperv template needs only an admin password; provider installs OpenSSH

Update the requirements, bootstrap contract, and lifecycle to reflect that
the provider now installs the OpenSSH server in the guest over PowerShell
Direct, so a template only needs a reachable administrator account rather
than a pre-baked OpenSSH setup. Adds a short "Preparing a template" recipe.

* fix: lock down administrators_authorized_keys ACL so admin SSH auth works

Found via live proof: a freshly provisioned lease reached SSH port 22 with
OpenSSH installed, but key auth failed (timeout at ports=22:auth). Cause:
when injecting the key for an administrator account, the
administrators_authorized_keys file inherits an ACL that grants
"Authenticated Users" read access. Windows OpenSSH refuses to honor that
file unless it is restricted to SYSTEM + Administrators with inheritance
disabled, so the key was silently ignored.

injectSSHKey now runs `icacls <file> /inheritance:r /grant SYSTEM:F
BUILTIN\Administrators:F` right after writing the admin keys file.

Verified live: with the ACL locked down, `ssh -i <key> Administrator@<vm>`
authenticates and runs commands. Adds a regression test.

* feat: back Hyper-V leases with a differencing disk instead of copying the VHDX

Each lease previously did a full Copy-Item of the template VHDX (~42 GB,
~8 min on a fast NVMe), dominating provision time. Replace that with a
per-lease differencing disk over the template
(New-VHD -Differencing -ParentPath): near-instant, space-thin (the lease
only stores its own writes), and the template stays read-only and shared
across leases. This is Hyper-V's equivalent of tart's APFS copy-on-write
clone.

The lease inherits the template's virtual size, so the per-lease
Resize-VHD (and its grow-only guard) is removed -- size the template
instead. On release only the child differencing disk is deleted; the
template is untouched. Updates tests and docs.

* feat: install git in the guest so a plain Windows template just works

Crabbox's Windows SSH-readiness check requires git (for sync), but a base
Windows VHDX (e.g. the MS dev image) often lacks it -- so warmup reached
SSH but timed out at the readiness command. Mirroring how the Linux
cloud-init path installs git, the provider now installs git (portable
MinGit from the latest git-for-windows release) over PowerShell Direct
when it is absent, alongside the OpenSSH install. Idempotent: a no-op when
git is already present, so a template that pre-bakes it skips the
per-lease download.

With this, a plain Windows template needs only a known administrator
password -- the provider supplies OpenSSH + git. Verified live: warmup
--provider hyperv reaches state=ready (ssh=Administrator@<ip>,
workroot=C:\crabbox). Adds a test; updates docs.

* feat: register --hyperv-user and --hyperv-work-root flags

The docs/quickstart referenced --hyperv-user, but only the YAML/env paths
set it, so a documented CLI invocation failed flag parsing. Register
--hyperv-user and --hyperv-work-root (the guest password stays off the
command line -- it is only read from CRABBOX_HYPERV_GUEST_PASSWORD).
Adds a test; verified `--hyperv-user` parses.

feat(providers): add Phala confidential TDX CVM SSH-lease provider (#367)

* feat(providers): add Phala confidential TDX CVM SSH-lease provider

Add phala as a Linux-only ProviderKindSSHLease instance provider, adapted
from the namespaceinstance template. It leases a Phala Cloud / dstack
confidential Intel TDX CVM via the phala CLI (deploy --dev-os --ssh-pubkey
--wait), SSHes in over crabbox's normal sync/run path, and releases with
cvms delete. First confidential/attested execution substrate in crabbox.

Scope: lease/run/release only. TDX attestation (cvms attestation) is
deferred and intentionally not advertised -- crabbox has no confidential
Feature constant yet.

- internal/providers/phala: provider/flags/backend (+ tests)
- internal/cli/phala_proxy.go: SSH gateway proxy shim (__phala-proxy)
- internal/cli/config.go: PhalaConfig + file/env wiring
- docs/providers/phala.md + regenerated provider matrix
- scripts/live-phala-smoke.sh: guarded live smoke

Ownership is anchored on the local claim (Phala exposes no server-side
labels), so List/Cleanup/ReleaseLease never touch a name-prefixed CVM that
lacks a matching local crabbox claim.

* fix(phala): align deploy + SSH with Phala CLI contract (PR #367 review)

- deploy always supplies --compose (bundled default compose; the phala
  CLI requires a compose file in non-interactive mode)
- SSH proxy uses the dstack TLS gateway: derive <appId>-22.<gateway-domain>
  from the cvms get gateway object and tunnel via openssl s_client (was
  raw TCP on flat host/port fields); openssl is now a host dependency
- tests for compose-always-present + gateway-host derivation + openssl tunnel

* phala: parse real CLI JSON shapes from live TDX hardware

The live lease->run->release run against real Phala TDX hardware revealed
the actual `phala` CLI output contract, which the provider mis-parsed:

- deploy --json prints a leading "Provisioning CVM <name>..." progress
  line before the JSON object; jsonObjectPrefix only trimmed trailing
  noise, so deploy failed with "produced no JSON output". Now scans to
  the first top-level { and tolerates leading AND trailing noise.
- cvms list items use camelCase keys (appId/vmUuid/instanceId); cvms get
  uses snake_case (app_id/vm_uuid). instance now decodes BOTH spellings
  via a custom UnmarshalJSON; cloudID() prefers app_id (the confirmed
  --cvm-id handle for get/delete).
- listInstances skips items with no usable name/handle instead of failing.

Tests parse the exact observed deploy stdout, camelCase list payload, and
snake_case cvms-get/gateway payload.

* phala: bootstrap the immutable dstack dev-os guest (drop hard git requirement)

Live SSH into a real --dev-os TDX CVM showed the dstack guest is an
immutable confidential-compute appliance: read-only squashfs root, no
package manager (apt/dnf/yum/apk all absent), no network egress. It already
ships rsync, tar and python3 -- everything crabbox's rsync-based sync and
exec needs -- but NOT git. The earlier bootstrap required git, so it could
never succeed on the supported guest and failed live with
"Phala CVM tool bootstrap failed: exit status 1" after SSH auth.

crabbox does not need git on the box (the file manifest is computed locally
and the working tree is rsync'd, not git-cloned, over the SSH gateway
tunnel). So the required tool set is now rsync+tar+python3; git is installed
only opportunistically when a package manager exists (non-dev-os images) and
is never required. The lease ReadyCheck drops git for the same reason.

Tests pin the dev-os contract: rsync+tar+python3 required, git opportunistic.

* phala: default work root to writable /var/volatile (dev-os root is read-only)

Second live finding: after bootstrap succeeded the run reached the sync
step and failed at "write sync manifests: exit status 1". The dstack
--dev-os guest roots its filesystem on a read-only squashfs (confirmed via
mount: /dev/mapper/rootfs on / type squashfs ro), so the /work/crabbox work
root could not be mkdir'd. /var/volatile is a writable tmpfs present on
every dstack guest.

Default Phala work root is now /var/volatile/crabbox (BaseConfig and the
applyDefaults fallback). ValidateConfig additionally rejects the bare
/var/volatile mount as too broad, matching the existing /tmp, /var, /work
guards. Docs and the deploy-args test updated; tests pin the writable
default and that it survives its own validator. Users needing encrypted
at-rest persistence can point --phala-work-root at
/var/volatile/dstack/persistent/...

(The earlier git-requirement and JSON-shape fixes already landed; this is
the remaining writable-path gap before the live smoke completes.)

* phala: anchor ownership on local claim, not absent server labels

Live release/resolve revealed the ownership model relied on server-side
labels that Phala never provides: cvms list returns no crabbox labels and
omits even the CVM name (only cvms get/deploy/delete echo the name). The
run failed at resolve with "ownership labels do not match lease".

Rework, consistent with Phala's reality that the local lease claim (which
records the CVM cloud id at acquire time) is the ownership authority:

- owned(): dual-proof -- a local claim maps to the CVM cloud id (post-acquire
  authority, the reliable path for List/Resolve where cvms list has no name),
  OR the CVM name carries the crabbox-<lease> prefix (pre-claim recovery of
  our own just-created CVM, before the claim is written).
- phalaLabels(): synthesize lease/slug/owner from the claim keyed on the CVM
  cloud id, falling back to the crabbox- name prefix for objects that do carry
  a name (cvms get).
- Resolve claim branch: trust the claim (owned re-resolves it by cloud id)
  instead of cross-checking absent server labels.
- Destructive ops (validateDestroyTarget) source the CVM -- and its name --
  from cvms get (which carries it on real hardware) rather than cvms list,
  then corroborate: require a local claim AND a crabbox-<lease> name matching
  the lease. This preserves the four release-safety properties (reject
  foreign-named, mismatched-lease, unclaimed, and skip-when-gone) against the
  app-id-reuse threat, now working on real Phala instead of only on mocked
  list payloads with names.

Adds getInstance (cvms get) and tests pinning the real get/list shapes.

* phala: cache the TLS gateway host so SSH skips per-connection cvms get

The __phala-proxy ProxyCommand resolved the dstack gateway host by calling
`phala cvms get` on EVERY SSH connection. crabbox status --wait uses a 4s
SSH readiness probe (probeSSHReady) that cannot complete cvms-get + openssl
TLS + SSH in 4s, so it timed out ("timed out waiting for <lease> to become
ready") even though the leased CVM was up -- the live run path tolerates it
via a longer wait, but every connection paid an extra API round-trip.

The gateway host (<app_id>-22.<gateway_domain>) is stable for a CVM, so it is
now resolved ONCE at acquire (resolveGatewayHost via cvms get) and cached in
the lease claim under gateway_host. proxyCommand bakes --gateway-host into the
__phala-proxy invocation; the proxy tunnels straight to it and skips cvms get.
lease() reads the cached host from the claim-backed labels. When the cache is
absent (older claims, resolution failure) the proxy falls back to cvms get, so
behavior degrades gracefully.

This makes status --wait succeed, cuts an API call + latency off every SSH
connection, and reduces Phala API load. Tests cover the cached-host fast path
(no cvms get), the fallback, real cvms-get gateway parsing, and the
acquire->claim->proxy round-trip.

* phala: enforce TLS server auth on the SSH gateway tunnel (close MITM)

The SSH gateway tunnel runs `openssl s_client` with only -verify_quiet,
which merely restricts verify OUTPUT -- a certificate-chain failure did NOT
abort the connection. Combined with SSH host-key checking being disabled
(the per-lease CVM host key is unknown), the TLS handshake was the only
server authentication AND it enforced nothing: a network MITM between the
crabbox host and <appId>-22.<gateway-domain>:443 could terminate TLS with any
cert, read the SSH session, and inject commands -- defeating the confidential
-compute trust boundary the provider exists to uphold.

Add -verify_return_error (abort on any chain-verification failure) and
-verify_hostname <host> (pin the leaf cert to the gateway host so a valid-
chain cert for a different name cannot be substituted). The dstack gateway
presents a publicly-trusted cert for the gateway host (verified live against
the ambient trust store), so genuine connections still succeed. Proxy test
now asserts both flags are present.

* phala: address adversarial review + live lifecycle findings

Parse the real cvms-list name key and fix ownership/lifecycle gaps surfaced
by an independent adversarial review and live TDX testing:

- cvms list items carry the name under `cvmName` (camelCase), not name/appName
  -- instance.UnmarshalJSON now reads it, restoring ambiguous-create recovery,
  owned()'s name branch, and name surfacing; all list-shaped test fixtures
  corrected to the real keys (appId/cvmName/status).
- Cleanup now routes every live delete through validateDestroyTarget (cvms get
  name corroboration), matching ReleaseLease, so a stale claim onto a reused
  app_id can no longer delete a foreign CVM (P1).
- destroy()/getInstance() no longer treat any 'not found' substring (incl over
  err.Error()) as success; an anchored missingCVMResponse helper distinguishes
  a definitively-absent CVM from a transient lookup failure, and ReleaseLease
  retains the claim+key on an ambiguous failure instead of orphaning a live
  billing CVM (P2).
- status --wait no longer re-runs the full prepareSSH bootstrap (Resolve gates
  prepareSSH on !StatusOnly), so it relies on the lightweight readiness probe.
- slug now round-trips through the claim (acquire injects it; Resolve/Touch
  re-claims preserve it) so resolve/status/stop by slug work and list shows it.
- configuration.md workRoot corrected to /var/volatile/crabbox; gateway app-id
  resolver aligned with the proxy; ambiguous-create markers anchored.

Adds tests pinning the real cvms-list cvmName shape, the Cleanup foreign-reuse
refusal, transient-not-found claim retention, ReleaseLease positive destroy
(mutation-checked), Acquire rollback-destroy, slug round-trip, status-only
no-bootstrap, and the gateway-domain preference table.

* phala: verify Intel TDX attestation before trusting a leased CVM

A confidential-compute provider must prove the box is a genuine attested
enclave running the authorized code -- not just an SSH-reachable VM. After
the CVM is reachable, Acquire now fetches the dstack guest-agent attestation
over SSH (/var/run/tappd.sock Tappd.Info -> app_cert + tcb_info) and verifies,
against the app id of the CVM it just deployed:

- RTMR replay: recompute RTMR0..3 as the SHA-384 fold of the tcb_info event
  log and require they equal the hardware registers (the measurement is
  genuine and unforgeable -- a tampered event breaks it).
- quote consistency: extract the Intel TDX quote embedded in the app_cert
  (X.509 ext OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.62397.1.1) and require its TD-report MRTD/RTMRs
  equal tcb_info.
- DCAP signature: verify.TdxQuote (go-tdx-guest) chains the quote to the Intel
  SGX/TDX Root CA -- genuine Intel silicon, not an emulator.
- identity binding: the RTMR3 event log's app-id must equal the deployed CVM's
  app id, so the attested enclave is OUR deployment.

On failure the just-created CVM is destroyed (never leaked) and the lease is
refused; on success the verified app-id/compose-hash/rtmr3 are surfaced in the
lease labels (attested=true). Gate defaults ON (--phala-skip-attestation to
opt out); untrusted repo config may only tighten it, never disable.

Tests run against a REAL attestation captured off live TDX hardware
(testdata/): RTMR replay match + mutation-breaks, quote<->tcb_info MRTD/RTMR
equality, app-id binding (+wrong-id rejection), and an opt-in network DCAP
test (CRABBOX_TDX_DCAP_NETWORK_TEST=1) that chains the real quote to Intel.

* phala: persist non-repo acquire claims; correct attestation docs (ClawSweeper)

Address the ClawSweeper re-review of the attestation commit:

- [P1] Acquire's success path called ClaimLeaseTargetForRepoConfig
  unconditionally, which no-ops when req.Repo.Root is empty. Phala ownership is
  anchored on the local claim, so a non-repo acquire (warmup, or run outside a
  repo) returned a live, billing CVM that List/stop/Cleanup could never find or
  destroy. Extracted claimAcquiredLease() which falls back to
  ClaimLeaseTargetForConfig when there is no repo root; test pins that a
  non-repo (and whitespace) repo root still writes a resolvable claim.
- [P3] docs/providers/phala.md still described attestation as deferred/not
  verified; rewrote the section to document the default-on Acquire gate
  (RTMR replay + quote consistency + DCAP-to-Intel-root + app-id binding) and
  the --phala-skip-attestation opt-out, added attest to the config example,
  corrected the provider-metadata caveat, and regenerated the provider matrix.

* phala: extract parseDstackInfo for deterministic attestation-fetch coverage

Mutation testing (gremlins, 100% efficacy / 0 survivors over the package)
flagged the dstack Info parsing inside fetchAttestation as uncovered because
it was welded to the SSH fetch. Split the deterministic parse (trim, skip a
leading shell banner to the first '{', JSON-decode, reject empty) into
parseDstackInfo; fetchAttestation keeps only the SSH call (the genuine seam
gap). TestParseDstackInfo covers clean/bannered/whitespace inputs and the
empty + non-JSON rejections.

feat: add watch command for warm-lease reruns on local file changes (#791)

* feat: add watch command for warm-lease reruns on local file changes

Adds crabbox watch, a live edit-save-rerun loop on a warm lease. Each
iteration calls the existing run path with an injected --id and a
deterministic watch #N label, so sync fingerprints, history, results,
artifacts, and attach behave exactly as for run. Reruns queue and
coalesce while a run is active, at most one pending. Filesystem events
are qualified against the exact sync universe and the loop idle-exits
after a period bounded by the lease idle timeout.

Direction and v1 contract approved by the maintainer in
https://github.com/openclaw/crabbox/issues/784

* feat: honor sync.include whitelist in watch event qualification

With a sync.include whitelist configured, changes outside the included
trees are not part of the sync universe, so they no longer trigger
reruns or reset the idle-exit timer. pathIncluded is applied at the
same layer syncManifestFiltered applies it: on git ls-files output and
on qualified deletions.

* fix: re-attach watches when a filter reload relaxes directory exclusions

Startup skips excluded directories in addWatchTree, so a mid-session
.crabboxignore or config edit that removes an exclusion updated the
filters but left the newly included subtree unwatched; edits inside it
were invisible until restart. When a reloaded exclude list differs, the
watcher re-walks the repository root; fsnotify Add is idempotent for
directories that are already watched.

* fix: run a queued rerun before honoring idle exit

A qualifying change during a long iteration queued a rerun and reset
the idle timer, but when the iteration outlasted the idle-exit window
the timer re-fired and the completion path returned before starting the
queued rerun, silently dropping the promised coalesced run. Pending
work now starts first; the sticky idle-exit flag still ends the loop
after that run unless new qualifying activity arrives during it.

feat!: replace Code-Hex/vz with a native Swift VM daemon and rename apple-vz to apple-vm (#872)

* feat: replace Code-Hex/vz with native Swift VM daemon

The apple-vz helper is now pure Go (CGO_ENABLED=0) and spawns
crabbox-apple-vm-vmd, a dependency-free Swift daemon that owns all
Virtualization.framework work (VM hosting, vsock SSH proxy, doctor
probe). The helper installs and codesigns the daemon itself, so the
backend's managed-helper copy/codesign machinery is gone.

* feat!: rename apple-vz provider to apple-vm and wire Swift daemon build

Provider, helper binary, packages, config keys, flags, env vars, and
docs move to apple-vm naming. Old names remain deprecated aliases:
provider aliases apple-vz/applevz, appleVZ config key, --apple-vz-*
flags, CRABBOX_APPLE_VZ_* env vars. Claim lookups canonicalize stored
provider names and the apple-vz state directory migrates on first use.
goreleaser/CI now build the Swift daemon and embed it into the pure-Go
helper (-tags vmdembed); helper gains vmd-info for packaging checks.

* fix: correct helper stub build tag and stale JS release-contract tests

The cli_stub.go !cgo guard collided with the pure-Go helper build
(CGO_ENABLED=0 selected both RunCLI definitions); the stub now covers
non darwin/arm64 platforms only. scripts/release-workflow.test.js and
live-smoke.test.js now assert the embedded-daemon release contract and
apple-vm naming.

* fix: define VMD constants in cross-platform helper file

VMDPathEnv/ManagedVMDName were declared in a darwin/arm64-only file but
referenced from the always-built provider backend, breaking Linux and
Windows builds.

* fix: keep daemon teardown from overwriting terminal VM status

Stopping the loopback proxy during finish() surfaces as an accept error;
fail() now ignores callbacks after a terminal state so a clean stop is
not rewritten to status=error.

* test: drop dead codesign call counter left from managed-helper tests

* fix: keep HelperDir beside its darwin-only callers

Only the darwin/arm64 managed-daemon installer uses it now, so the
Linux deadcode gate flagged it in the cross-platform protocol file.

* fix: declare archive-sync feature for daytona provider

Daytona syncs by streaming a gzipped tar archive through the Daytona
toolbox API, and docs/providers/provider-metadata.json already records
sync=archive-sync, but the provider spec declared crabbox-sync. The
generated provider matrix row was self-contradictory (sync archive-sync
vs features crabbox-sync), crabbox doctor required rsync which the
backend never uses, and the delegated-run option gate rejected
--sync-only and --force-sync-large even though the backend implements
both.

Declare FeatureArchiveSync, allow archive-sync on SSH-lease hybrids in
the kind/feature contract, extend the sync-option gate conformance test
to cover them, and validate metadata sync against declared features in
generate-provider-matrix.mjs so this drift class fails check-docs.sh.

warmup -> status --wait -> list -> stop, with zero residual instances

fix(worker): drain container-runner pipes idle-aware with an absolute cap (#1097)

Own-pipe cmd.Wait ordering (from the earlier fix) still had a fixed
5s pipeDrainGrace select after cmd.Wait: a quiet background
descendant that inherited a write-end (e.g. `sleep 30 & echo done`)
forced every such request to pay the full grace latency, even though
there was nothing left to drain (measured: 0.2s baseline vs 5.1s).

Replace the fixed select with an idle-aware drain. copyPipe now adds
every byte it copies to a shared atomic counter. After cmd.Wait, a
poll loop returns as soon as: the copiers hit a real EOF (no
descendant); `copied` makes no progress for pipeDrainIdle (300ms,
polled every pipeDrainPoll=100ms) — a quiet/absent descendant with
nothing left to lose; or the absolute pipeDrainGrace cap (5s) elapses
regardless of progress — bounding a descendant that writes
continuously (e.g. a busy-loop `echo`) and would otherwise keep
resetting the idle timer forever. All three are vars so tests can
lower them.

Rewrite the background-descendant regression test to assert prompt
return (well under half the grace) instead of merely "not ~30s" —
this fails against the prior fixed-grace design (~5.1s) and passes
against the idle-aware drain (~0.5-0.7s observed over repeated runs).
Add a noisy-descendant test proving the absolute cap still bounds a
continuously-writing descendant, and a bursty-descendant test proving
the idle timer resets on progress instead of using one fixed deadline,
so a slow-but-live stream is never truncated.

Verification: go build/vet clean at repo root and in the runner
module; go test -race -run TestRunCommand -count=3 all green (25.3s);
gofmt clean.

(*backend).Cleanup snapshotted containers before reading lease claims, then its
orphan sweep removed -- via the unguarded core.RemoveLeaseClaim -- any claim
absent from the stale container view. A claim registered by a concurrent Acquire

fix(cp): prefer secluded rsync args for resolved SSH copies (#1162)

* fix(cp): prefer secluded rsync args for resolved SSH copies

The ssh-localhost connector smoke failed intermittently at "cp download
over resolved SSH" with the remote sender reporting a corrupted path:

  rsync: [sender] link_stat ".../workroot/cp remote[1].txtU" failed

The trailing byte is not ours. rsync 3.4.4's safe_arg() counts a
backslash as needing escape but intentionally does not double a
backslash that precedes a wildcard in a filename arg (exactly what
rsyncRemoteCopyPath produces for literal "[", "*", "?"), then NUL
terminates at the counted length. That leaves one uninitialized heap
byte inside the shell-transported arg; whenever the byte is non-zero
(0x55 = "U" on the failing runner) the remote shell receives a mangled
path. rsync 3.4.0-3.4.3 zeroed allocations, which masked the bug;
3.4.4 reverted that zeroing, and older 3.2.x/3.3.x lines are exposed
the same way.

Route around the whole class: probe the remote rsync for secluded-args
support (the same probe WSL2 targets already require) and pass
--secluded-args whenever the remote supports it, so remote paths travel
over the rsync protocol stream and never appear on the remote shell
command line. Remotes without secluded support (macOS openrsync, ancient
rsync) keep the previous shell-transported behavior.

Verified in an ubuntu:24.04 container mirroring CI (pinned rsync 3.4.4
client, distro rsync 3.2.7 remote): with client-side malloc poisoned to
0x55, the old binary reproduces the smoke failure deterministically and
the fixed binary passes the full smoke.

* test(cp): deflake SSH descendant reaping and pid-file waits

The SSH cp cancellation tests checked descendant teardown with a single
immediate syscall.Kill(pid, 0) ESRCH probe, but process-group reaping after

* test: fix flaky TestEgressDaemonConcurrentStartDoubleProvision

stopDaemonProcess signals the supervisor process group with SIGKILL, which
the kernel delivers asynchronously, so stopEgressHostDaemon can return
stopped=true while the supervisor is still tearing down. The test then
checked liveness the instant stop returned, so under CI load it
occasionally observed the not-yet-dead process and failed with
"supervisor pid remained alive after stop".

Poll for teardown with a bounded 3s timeout instead of asserting death
synchronously. SIGKILL is guaranteed to terminate the process, so this is
deterministic; a reaped or zombie process already reads as dead via
egressDaemonTestAlive. Test-only change; production stop semantics are
unchanged.

fix(hyperv): provisioning hangs while Windows guests boot (#1175)

* fix(hyperv): provisioning hangs forever waiting for PowerShell Direct

A new Hyper-V lease could hang indefinitely during provisioning. After
Start-VM, the first guest call (PowerShell Direct via stageSSHKey) fires while
the guest is still booting, where `Invoke-Command -VMName` blocks instead of
fast-failing, and no per-attempt timeout let the fixed retry loop advance. The
whole `crabbox run` then stalls with no progress. This has been latent since the
provider was introduced in #212.

Add a bounded PowerShell Direct readiness gate (`waitGuestReady`) before the
first guest call: it retries a trivial authenticated probe within an overall
budget, with each attempt bounded so a blocked probe is killed and retried
(verified not to corrupt the guest session). Every real guest call
(`invokeInGuest`) also gets a generous per-attempt timeout so a wedged
mid-session call can never hang the provision.

Also fix guest OpenSSH install: `Add-WindowsCapability` (Features-on-Demand)
fails 0x800f0950 on templates without Windows Update access, so a plain template
could never finish provisioning. Install the pinned, SHA-256-verified
Win32-OpenSSH MSI (the Microsoft.OpenSSH.Preview payload) from GitHub instead,
mirroring how git is bootstrapped, and resolve sshd/ssh-keygen from the sshd
service path since the MSI installs to C:\Program Files\OpenSSH rather than
System32\OpenSSH.

* docs(hyperv): document bootstrap requirements

Align the repo-local Crabbox skill and Hyper-V provider reference with the bounded PowerShell Direct readiness gate and pinned Win32-OpenSSH MSI bootstrap.

feat(providers): report machine class shapes in the provider matrix (#1396)

Machine classes are provider-neutral intent labels, so the concrete size a
class resolves to was only discoverable by reading the docs. `providers --json`
now carries an optional `classes` array per provider with the primary instance
type each class resolves to plus its nominal vCPU count and RAM.

A new optional ProviderClassSpecProvider hook keeps per-provider shape
knowledge in each provider package instead of extending the core
provider-class if-chain. Implemented for aws, azure, gcp, hetzner and
namespace-instance; other providers emit no classes key.

Shapes are derived from the existing class tables rather than hardcoded per
class. GCP uses quarter-GB units because c4-standard is 3.75 GB/vCPU, and a
non-divisible result omits memory rather than rounding. Unknown families

feat(machine0): support fixed idempotent lease IDs (#1414)

* feat(machine0): support fixed idempotent lease IDs

Automation that derives one canonical lease identity and replays it after a
lost response could not use Machine0: warmup rejected --lease-id unless the
backend implemented IdempotentLeaseIDBackend, so it exited 2 before any
allocation.

Machine0 exposes no cloud-side tags, so the AWS attestation scheme does not
port over directly. The binding instead uses the two identities Machine0 does
provide: the deterministic VM name derived from the lease ID and allocated
slug, and the Machine0 resource ID. The durable create intent is bound to the
name before creation; the create attempt is persisted before `machine0 new`;
and every later adoption must match the exact recorded resource ID. A matching
name or slug alone never authorizes reuse.

Replay fails closed without a second create while a pinned attempt has no
visible machine, accepting the same deliberate false negative as AWS to keep
at-most-once creation. Because `machine0 new` can fail for ordinary capacity
reasons, a definite failure is established by a bounded 60s inventory
reconcile rather than by the error alone, so a real failure stays retryable
without wedging the lease. Once creation may have succeeded the fixed path
never rolls the VM back, since the caller's identity is bound to it.

Destroy release replaces the claim with a compact terminal tombstone under the
downgrade-safe `machine0-fixed-v1` discriminator, making fixed IDs single-use;
suspend release keeps the live claim so replay restarts the exact machine.

lease-ID validation. Extract the engine into shared as a three-tier API
(LockLeaseOperation / LockOperation / LockOperationFile) so providers keep
their own validation, slug-allocation locks, and claim-namespace
preparation while the locking mechanics exist once.

On-disk lock paths are preserved byte-for-byte and pinned by a test
carrying all nine literal legacy filenames, so old and new binaries

created sandbox/session even when --keep-on-failure requested retention;

paths so they are built exactly once; the snapshot is immune to workspace

chore: stabilize cancellation tests under suite load

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves timing-dependent assumptions in two cancellation tests that were observed failing during complete local Go race sweeps but passing in isolated repetitions. The tests should detect broken cancellation, not incidental scheduling or persistence latency.

## Why This Change Was Made

The controller test now uses a controlled test clock, publishes the actual cleanup context as its readiness notification, verifies cleanup is still active before cancellation, and independently bounds shutdown completion. Its old one-second startup guard included reconciliation scheduling and durable state writes before provider cleanup started.

The OpenSandbox test distinguishes timeout before versus after init consumption. It preserves the real HTTP client/server and SDK endpoint-discovery/interruption paths over an in-memory connection. Both cases require the exact existing 20 ms deadline and HTTP cancellation; the known-ID case requires exactly one DELETE. Server-side flushing is not treated as client-side readiness.

## User Impact

No CLI or provider behavior changes. This is test-only: production deadlines, cancellation guarantees, dependencies, configuration, and credentials are unchanged. No changelog entry is needed.

## Evidence

Controlled local probes reproduced the original controller startup assertion in 3/3 runs and the OpenSandbox empty-ID assertion in 10/10 runs. The fixed controller test passed 3/3 runs with a verified 1.1-second external persistence delay. Negative controls fail when startup, cancellation propagation, shutdown completion, streaming deadlines, or interruption-context independence are broken. These establish weaknesses in the tests' timing assumptions, not the exact ordering of the historical full-suite failures.

Completed local race verification:

- Controller target: 50 repetitions at CPU settings 1, 2, and 4 (150 runs), passed.
- Six neighboring controller cancellation/reconciliation tests: 10 repetitions each, passed.
- OpenSandbox timing test: 100 repetitions at CPU settings 1, 2, and 4 (600 subtest executions), passed.
- Full OpenSandbox package, passed.
- Both target tests on cached Go 1.26.6: 10 repetitions each, passed.
- After rebasing onto current main, both target tests passed another 10 race repetitions.
- The pinned `deadcode@v0.45.0 -test ./...` gate produced no findings.
- `go vet ./internal/cli ./internal/providers/opensandbox`, `gofmt`, and `git diff --check`, passed.

Tests used task-owned HOME directories and an allowlisted environment with provider/credential/live-test inputs removed. `XDG_STATE_HOME` was not globally set, leaving fixture overrides in control. All provider operations were fake or local HTTP test operations. Raw logs and generated fixture credentials are not included.

The complete repository/full CLI race sweep was not rerun locally; CI covers the integrated branch. No live-provider or remote-platform proof is claimed.

fix: isolate coordinator acknowledgements from notification and scheduling failures

## Summary

Keep coordinator acknowledgements independent of failed control-socket notifications and full-fleet scheduling scans.

- Retire control sockets whose attachments cannot be read or serialized without failing an already-durable run/event acknowledgement. Ignore their delayed callbacks without affecting replacement sockets with the same client ID, and continue delivery to authorized subscribers.
- Arm alarms conservatively for ordinary HTTP/control heartbeats and lease releases instead of scanning global workspace/lease collections in those acknowledgement critical sections. Preserve earlier deadlines and durably queued cleanup; rearm overdue timestamps that can outlive consumed runtime jobs.
- Add synthetic regressions for exact terminal receipt/log recovery, idempotent/conflicting finish replay, subscriber authorization, delayed socket callbacks, bounded acknowledgement storage work, deadline preservation, reconstruction, and cleanup failures.

Receipt validation, storage failures, grant checks, lease identity/cleanup fencing, and provider cleanup semantics remain unchanged. No schema, configuration, credential, dependency, or permission changes.

## Verification

The new cases failed before their corresponding fixes. Final local verification on Node 24 passed:

- `npm test --prefix worker -- test/fleet.test.ts test/coordinator-runtime.test.ts test/node-runtime.test.ts test/run-receipt.test.ts` — 848 tests passed after rebase.
- `npm run check --prefix worker`
- `npm run check:node --prefix worker`
- Targeted `oxlint` and `oxfmt` for the changed source, tests, and documentation; full Worker lint and formatting checks also passed.
- Full Worker suite: 2,106 tests passed, 3 live-only tests skipped.
- Worker dry-run build, Cloudflare Dynamic Workers dry-run build, and Node runtime build passed.
- Focused Go tests for terminal receipt recovery, bookkeeping exit 7, release cancellation, and stop completion budgets.

## Scope and limitations

This fixes reproduced source-level acknowledgement defects; it does **not** establish the exact exception behind an observed Cloudflare 1101 incident. A native command can succeed while coordinator bookkeeping returns exit 7, and those outcomes must remain distinct. Identical committed finish replay already bypasses notification, so a socket failure alone does not explain repeated platform failures.

Full maintenance scans, provider ingress waits, and other queue owners retain their existing behavior. Proof is synthetic; no live lease operations or workerd cancellation/lifetime proof are claimed. The existing merge-triggered coordinator deployment is authorized for this landing; no separate manual deployment is included.

Release-note context: brokered runs no longer fail durable acknowledgement solely because a control subscriber attachment failed, and ordinary lease heartbeats/releases avoid global alarm-reconciliation scans on their acknowledgement path.

fix(coordinator): preserve earlier wakeups after maintenance failures

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where failed background maintenance could replace an already-armed coordinator wakeup with a later retry. It also reconciles transaction-aware acknowledgement fixtures from concurrent changes while preserving strict failure and rollback coverage, and removes host-timing false failures from two Go cancellation tests.

This is an integration follow-up to https://github.com/openclaw/crabbox/pull/1762 and https://github.com/openclaw/crabbox/pull/1766. The original Go-test change and the necessary coordinator repair are kept in separate commits.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Arm maintenance retries under the lifecycle mutex through the existing no-later-than helper, so a newer, earlier acknowledgement wake is preserved. Surface retry-arm failure instead of claiming a retry was scheduled.
- Reuse an unchanged future native alarm, while still rearming due/overdue timestamps that may outlive their consumed jobs. Keep due records and native alarms transactional.
- Observe and inject fixture failures at transaction boundaries, publish fake queued-alarm state only after commit, and seed coherent logical/native scheduling state. Preserve strict rollback, cleanup, reconstruction, and bounded-scan assertions rather than relaxing them to match broken spies.
- Measure the Go grace/rollback cancellation contracts with virtual time while retaining the real fake-SSH commands and acquisition bookkeeping. Join completion before inspecting captured stderr.

## User Impact

Coordinator maintenance retries no longer postpone earlier queued work after a maintenance failure. Contributors also get deterministic cancellation regression coverage on loaded hosts. Public APIs, configuration, schemas, credentials, dependencies, permissions, and timeout values are unchanged.

## Evidence

The combined candidate passed local verification with Node 24:

One additional native-alarm-read failure case verifies that the callback does not run and durable data, the legacy deadline, and queued work remain unchanged. Coverage includes injected transaction/alarm failures, serialization conflict, consumed-job repair, unchanged-future-alarm reuse, and earlier-wakeup preservation.
- Worker formatting, lint, both typechecks, both Worker dry-run builds, Node build, and image-pin validation passed. Docker image construction remains for hosted CI.
- Both Go cancellation tests passed normally and five times with race detection during local preparation: **12 passes**, no race warnings. Their source and relevant production functions are unchanged by the fixture reconciliation. Four temporary mutation controls correctly rejected doubled/missing rollback bounds, inherited caller cancellation, and ignored grace cancellation.
- An identical 1.2-second fake-SSH startup delay reproduced the original missing-log failure; the corrected test passed while still requiring exactly one second of virtual cancellation time.

## Summary

Add an explicit read-only cleanup diagnostic for brokered Azure leases. Previously, a retained cleanup claim could disagree with live Azure resources while the public lease record exposed only `observed resource identity changed`, leaving operators unable to inspect the exact mismatch without direct provider credentials or storage access.

`GET /v1/leases/{id}/cleanup` uses the existing owner/manage-share/admin authorization and a provider-neutral inspection hook. The Azure adapter reads the retained baseline/deletion progress and the four canonical resource identities in the original subscription/resource group, not current deployment defaults. It reports concurrent claim changes without creating, updating, clearing, or accepting a claim. View-only shares, device credentials, unrelated users, registered leases, and unsupported providers do not gain provider access.

The response excludes resource bodies, raw tags, bootstrap data, credentials, and operation URLs. Stable-identity agreement and ownership classification remain distinct diagnostics: neither grants deletion authority. The existing cleanup/delete path is unchanged.

fix(azure): recover audited missing-IP cleanup debt (#1893)

## Summary

Fix Azure Location-style long-running-operation completion and add a narrowly scoped, explicitly authorized recovery for historical cleanup debt. A missing public-IP completion entry can otherwise strand an original detached disk after VM/NIC deletion, even when the remaining disk's identity and ownership still match.

The recovery is **not automatic absence acceptance or a recovered Azure DELETE receipt**. An owner/admin must explicitly acknowledge original-scope public-IP absence using the exact inspected claim fingerprint. The adapter requires an expired blocked lease, a complete ordinary v2 baseline and recorded VM/NIC deletion, four fresh canonical resource reads, and only the exact original owned detached disk in the original region. It rejects pending work, replacements, ownership/attachment changes, incomplete/quarantined claims, retained-resource disposition, and stale lease/claim state.

A short lease fence and fingerprint-CAS transaction preserve the immutable baseline and actual DELETE receipts while storing a separate audit and promoting the claim to v3. Older workers fail closed. Only ordinary release consumes this recovery, rechecks survivors, and deletes the original disk; the acknowledgement request itself performs no cloud mutation. The audit survives completion and remains visible through cleanup diagnostics. Inspection/provider reads run outside the lifecycle queue to avoid lock re-entry.

Separately, Azure-AsyncOperation remains a status-document protocol, while Location fallback can finish with terminal HTTP 200/204 without a top-level status. Pending 202, explicit failure/pending states, deadlines, and legacy missing-progress guards remain conservative. The historical original response is not available, so this prospective regression proof is not represented as proof of that incident's exact provider response.

## Verification

- Full Worker Vitest suite after integrating current main: **2,774 passed, 3 skipped**.
- Worker format, lint, and TypeScript checks; Node coordinator typecheck.
- Worker dry-run build, Node coordinator build, and Cloudflare Dynamic Workers build.
- Recovery tests cover rollback, concurrent/idempotent CAS, immutable baseline and actual receipt separation, retained audit, ordinary disk-only release, resource reappearance, generation/ownership/region/detachment refusals, v3 rollback/context fences, and owner/lease races at the final commit boundary.
- 29 new Location polling cases include owned cleanup progress only after terminal provider completion.
- Independent Codex review: **scoped-clean, no P0/P1 findings**.

No new credentials, roles, configuration, dependencies, direct cloud-delete command, or CLI publication is introduced. Live recovery and normal-stop verification follow the serialized coordinator deployment; this PR does not itself assert cloud cleanup has completed.

perf(bootstrap): reuse installed desktop packages on restored Linux images

## What Problem This Solves

Restoring a prepared Linux image repeated desktop package transactions and browser signing-key/repository downloads even when all required packages and a working browser were already installed. That adds avoidable work before a desktop lease becomes usable.

## Why This Change Was Made

Both bootstrap producers now use one shared package-state check. They skip an optional package transaction only when every required package is fully installed, including held installed packages. Browser reuse additionally requires a supported package and an executable that passes a bounded version probe. Missing or broken prerequisites keep the existing installation path and failure behavior.

## User Impact

Prepared desktop images avoid redundant package and browser setup work. Per-lease policies, wrappers, keys, ownership, service configuration, and final readiness checks still run. A working browser is retained at the image's installed version; operators update it when maintaining or rebaking the image. No standing capacity or new configuration is introduced.

## Evidence

The executable generated-bootstrap regression failed on the original code at a forbidden APT transaction and passes with this repair. Missing and unconfigured packages still trigger installation, installation failure propagates, and absent or broken browsers fail reuse.

Focused Go bootstrap tests, 45 Worker bootstrap tests, generator/parity checks, Worker typecheck/lint/dry-run build, documentation build, formatting, and diff checks passed. Independent Codex review through P2 found no actionable findings on the complete candidate. After refreshing over the current Windows bootstrap changes, the generated-fragment/parity suite passed all 24 checks, both Worker bootstrap suites passed 31 tests, and the focused Go bootstrap tests passed. The reviewed production patch is unchanged; the refresh preserved both changelog entries.

On a real AWS Linux prepared desktop, the exact candidate helper verified all requested installed desktop/browser packages and a working Chrome binary in 351 ms while a guard rejected any attempted package installation. The ordinary lease owner remained unchanged, and no service or workspace was modified. This is live capability-reuse proof, not a measured whole-VM boot speedup or a sub-ten-second cold-start claim.

A deterministic regression fails on the old implementation for success without creation and for output from a failing command. Both cases now preserve the existing gate and return BUSY. fix: share multipart producer and error ownership across providers

## Summary

Give Blaxel and the envd transport used by E2B/CubeSandbox one owner for multipart file production, pipe cancellation, and completion. A response can arrive before the request body finishes: returning then lets a retry rewind the archive or lets its caller close it while a producer still reads it. The shared callback-scoped helper always joins the producer before returning and never closes the borrowed source.

Adapters keep their HTTP endpoints, headers, redirects, retry policy, response interpretation, and error redaction. Primary exchange errors remain primary; a valid early response does not deliberately abort the upload. Source/finalization errors after an otherwise successful exchange are now reported rather than silently discarded by envd. Its existing success-response-body error policy is unchanged.

Consolidate three message/cause wrappers behind a small pointer-based helper. Provider secret selection and OpenSandbox's unchanged-message fast path stay local; the helper does not redact, select exit codes, or override errors.As. Using a pointer also avoids a reproduced errors.Is self-match panic with a legal non-comparable cause. CLI public-message/exit selection remains with its existing finalization owner.

Cancellation stops HTTP/pipe work but may await an in-flight noncooperative source Read; no universal bounded-read guarantee is claimed. Provider/architecture docs and the Unreleased changelog are updated. No dependencies, credentials, new settings, or native lifecycle/claim policy changes. This does not include the separate OpenSandbox timeout-budget work.

## Verification

- Blaxel baseline regression reproduced rewind before producer completion; its landed fix and exact retry-byte/ownership checks remain covered.
- Envd baseline reproduced early return, caller archive closure, and a subsequent read from that closed real file in three deterministic runs.
- Characterization distinguishes early success/source errors, HTTP/transport failures, cancellation, and the intentionally retained response-body policies.
- Controlled-reader tests verify completion before return, no borrowed Close, early success, cancellation and panic cleanup, error precedence, redaction, and multipart wire shape.
- The value-wrapper/non-comparable-cause panic was reproduced before the pointer fix. Tests retain typed causes, formatting, zero/signed inner exit selection, delegated classification, and unchanged-message identity.
- Full shared, Blaxel, E2B, CubeSandbox, and OpenSandbox race suites and vet passed after integration onto current main; independent P0-P2 review found no actionable issues.

These are exact reader, transport, and error-contract tests. They do not claim native cloud qualification. The finalized 0.65.0 notes and release authorization record are unchanged.

fix(opensandbox): bound execution and lifetime arithmetic

OpenSandbox multiplied configured timeout seconds into durations and added command, grace, and sync budgets without checking overflow. Large public inputs could turn the required lifetime negative and pass coverage admission; rounding a maximum valid TTL could also send negative lifetime seconds.

Use the existing checked seconds conversion and keep OpenSandbox's coupled budget policy in the provider. Reject unrepresentable execution and lifetime budgets before dispatch, check budget addition, and round TTL with quotient/remainder plus a platform integer-range check. Preserve defaults, earliest lifetime caps, sync-only/no-sync accounting, and absolute-expiry/resume/reclaim ordering. Status and stop retain their existing lifecycle admission; malformed persisted recovery lifetimes cannot authorize claim expiry. No new remote service cap, configuration, credentials, or error-wrapper change is introduced.

feat(proxmox): run the Proxmox provider behind adapter serve (#2577)

* feat(proxmox): run the Proxmox provider behind adapter serve

`crabbox adapter serve --provider proxmox` exited before listening with
"controller provider scope is empty", because Proxmox did not implement
the controller provider contract. Proxmox already supports replay-safe
fixed lease IDs, so this blocked every adapter lifecycle, including
headless Linux leases.

Proxmox now returns an opaque, non-secret controller scope: a SHA-256
digest of the normalized API endpoint, node, token ID, template, storage,
pool, bridge, clone mode, guest user and work root. It advertises fixed
lease IDs only for complete Linux configurations that fixed acquisition
accepts. That includes a non-blank token secret, so the adapter cannot
become ready with credentials that every lifecycle call would reject.

The secret is checked for presence only and never enters the scope, so it
can be replaced for the same token ID. Another token ID, route, node or
clone setting changes the scope. The existing persisted-scope check then
refuses lifecycle operations for workspaces created under the old scope
before any Proxmox client or request exists.

After release, the adapter's confirmed-absence cleanup must keep the
released fixed claim as the lease ID's receipt. Proxmox now validates that
receipt against both its controller scope and its claim scope, which
differ. Core confirmed-absence cleanup leaves the claim-scope comparison to
such a validator instead of comparing the receipt with the controller scope
itself. The Agent Sandbox validator already makes that comparison, and
claims without a receipt validator keep the core check. Without this, every
Proxmox adapter workspace stayed in `stopping` after its VM was deleted.

Direct provider behaviour is unchanged.

Related: https://github.com/openclaw/crabbox/issues/2558

* fix: keep coordinator registration in fixed release receipts

A registered runtime adapter releases a fixed-ID lease in two steps. `stop`
deletes the provider resource and replaces the claim with a compact
released receipt. Later, confirmed-absence cleanup completes the
coordinator's pending delete using the lease's registration generation.

`FixedLeaseKind.TerminalClaim` dropped `CoordinatorRegistrationURL`,
`RuntimeAdapterRegistrationID` and `RuntimeAdapterPendingRegistrationID`.
Cleanup therefore found no generation and fell back to the legacy
metadata release, which the coordinator rejects with
`runtime_adapter_delete_pending`. The VM was deleted, but the workspace
stayed `stopping` and the coordinator lease stayed active.

The receipt now keeps those three fields. Terminal validation against the
released claim rejects a receipt whose registration changed. Receipts
without registration, including those written before this change, stay
valid.

Related: https://github.com/openclaw/crabbox/issues/2558

controller scope. Give scope-drift failures an explicit restore-and-drain
recovery path without adding provider-specific controller logic.

fix: report unsupported native checkpoint modes precisely (#2613)

* fix: report unsupported native checkpoint modes precisely

A valid native checkpoint mode that capability resolution rejects (for
example a coordinator-brokered lease on a provider without brokered native
checkpoints) exited with the invalid-mode usage message and no JSON receipt,
so callers had to treat a deterministic refusal as an uncertain capture.

Invalid mode strings now fail before lease resolution. Unsupported native
modes exit 2 with a provider-neutral diagnostic naming the mode, strategy,
provider, target, and sanitized coordinator origin, and with --json emit a
crabbox.checkpoint.create.failure.v1 receipt with outcome not_submitted,
reason native_unsupported, and localReservation none. The refusal precedes
checkpoint create's own claim registration, retention probe, reservation,
source preparation, and checkpoint requests. The existing six-key receipt is
unchanged.
